title: Reading Compiler Errors
description: What an IDE does for you, and how to read a g++ error message instead of fearing it.

content.value: An **IDE** (Integrated Development Environment) is an editor built for programming. Visual Studio, CLion and VS Code are popular for C++.

content.real: A workshop with every tool on the wall
content.text: You could write C++ in any plain text editor and compile by typing commands. An IDE does the boring parts for you, so mistakes are cheaper to find.

items.sub: Text, numbers and keywords look different.
A missing brace is highlighted before you compile.

items.text: Compiles and runs in one step
items.sub: Here, Run or Ctrl+Enter does both.

content.value: The editor beside this lesson is a small IDE. It still can't stop every mistake, so reading error messages is the skill that matters.
A **compile error** means `g++` refused to build your code, so nothing ran at all. Read the message in order: where, then what.

content.title: Reading the message
content.caption: Below it, `g++` repeats your line and a `^` points at the exact spot.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: Add the `;` and it compiles and runs.

content.title: Broken vs fixed
content.caption: A missing `;` is reported at the start of the next line, so look at the end of the line just above.

content.question: You see `main.cpp:7:12: error: ...`. Which line do you look at first?
options: Line 12
Line 1
The last line of the file
Line 7
content.explain: After the file name comes the line (7), then the column (12). Go to line 7, then read what C++ expected.

items.sub: A semicolon is missing, usually at the end of the line above.
C++ doesn't know a name: usually a typo or a missing `#include`.

content.title: Three errors cover most of a beginner's week

items.text: `'cot' was not declared in this scope`

items.title: Exact name
items.text: C++ names must match letter for letter.

content.title: was not declared in this scope

content.value: Fix the **first** error, then compile again. One missing brace can cause a dozen complaints, and the later ones often vanish once the first is fixed.
content.title: First things first

content.value: A **warning** means `g++` built your program, but spotted something that looks like a mistake. Don't ignore warnings: in C++ they are often the bug you are about to hunt for an hour.
A **runtime error** is different: the code compiled, the program started, then something went wrong part way through.

steps.note: This line works, so `Starting up.` prints.
Dividing by zero has no answer. If this line ran, the program could stop right here, often with no helpful message. It is commented out so this version runs safely.
With the bad line switched off, the program carries on.

content.title: Where did it stop?
content.outro: C++ is not polite about runtime errors: you may only see `Segmentation fault`, or wrong values. The last line that printed is your clue: the problem is after it.

content.question: Your program prints two lines, then stops. What kind of error is it?
options: A runtime error
A compile error
A warning
Not an error
content.explain: If anything printed, the code compiled and started. It broke while running, so it is a runtime error.

content.title: When an error appears
content.caption: Change one thing at a time. If you change four things and the error goes away, you learn nothing about which one mattered.

output: Break me, then read the message.
content.caption: Fast programmers aren't the ones who avoid errors. They read them properly the first time.

content.question: You change four things at once and the error goes away. What is the problem?
options: You don't know which change fixed it
Nothing, that is the fastest way
The program will no longer compile
C++ undoes your changes
content.explain: Change one thing, run, and read. That way you learn exactly what each error means.

quiz.question: What is a compile error?
options: A mistake found before the program runs, so nothing runs.
A mistake that only happens on slow computers.
A mistake that appears halfway through running.
quiz.explain: `g++` checks first. If it reports an error, no executable is produced and the program never starts.

quiz.question: g++ says `main.cpp:7:5: error: expected ';' before 'return'`. Where do you look?
options: The first line of the file.
Anywhere: the line number is a rough guess.
Line 7, and the end of line 6 just above it.
quiz.explain: The numbers are line 7, column 5. A missing semicolon is reported where the compiler noticed it, which is often the start of the next line, so check the line above too.

quiz.question: Your program prints two lines and then stops without finishing. What kind of error is it?
options: A runtime error: it compiled and started, then broke.
A compile error: the code never compiled.
Both at once.
quiz.explain: Output appearing proves the code compiled and started running. Anything that goes wrong after that is a runtime error.

quiz.question: You have fifteen errors after one small change. What is the best next step?
options: Fix the last one, since it is the newest.
Fix the first one and compile again.
Undo everything you have written today.
quiz.explain: Errors cascade: one missing brace confuses everything after it. Fixing the first often clears most of the rest.

quiz.question: What does an IDE do for you?
options: Writes the program so you do not have to.
Makes errors impossible.
Colours code, spots mistakes early, suggests names, and runs your program.
quiz.explain: An IDE shortens the loop between writing and finding out. The thinking, and the reading of error messages, is still yours.
